title: KL flood hotspots cut by more than half from 2022 — minister - The Edge Malaysia
text:
KL flood hotspots cut by more than half from 2022 — minister Friday 20 Nov 2026 BURSA SGX Home 
 Make The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 19): Kuala Lumpur has reduced its flood hotspots from more than 30 in 2022 to 14 currently, with efforts underway to bring the number down to 10 by year end, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh said.
 She said the reduction was achieved through various flood mitigation measures, including improved rainwater management and enhanced preparedness for flash floods, as the city works towards becoming a Sponge City.
 Speaking at the official opening of HSBC Wealth Centre here on Thursday, Yeoh said Kuala Lumpur is also taking proactive measures to address flash floods, with live reports sent to the mayor whenever heavy rain occurred to facilitate monitoring and response efforts.
 The city is also developing on-site detention facilities, including underground rainwater storage facilities at Perdana Botanical Gardens and another beneath Padang Merbok, while monitoring more than 60 privately developed detention facilities across the city.
 “The facilities help temporarily store rainwater before releasing it gradually into the drainage system, reducing pressure on drains and rivers during heavy rainfall,” she said.
 Yeoh said protecting and preserving green spaces is also a priority, with a task force established to gazette parks to ensure they remain legally protected against future development.
 She noted that Kuala Lumpur had identified 32 green spaces for development under the microforest concept by 2027, as part of efforts to enhance the city’s resilience to climate change.
 Under Budget 2027, the city is also planning to develop 22km of covered pedestrian walkways across all 11 parliamentary constituencies in Kuala Lumpur to improve connectivity involving residential areas, public transport stations, schools, clinics and other public facilities.
 Yeoh said urban development must also take into account the needs of an ageing population, including providing platforms and programmes to address senior citizens’ social and lifestyle needs beyond healthcare and physical activities.
 She said older people also need companionship, opportunities to socialise and meaningful activities, adding that there is potential for more services and platforms tailored to their needs.
 On heritage conservation, she also said RM600 million had been committed through Khazanah Nasional Bhd for the restoration and conservation of important heritage buildings, including the Sultan Abdul Samad Building complex, Carcosa and Seri Negara.
 Yeoh added that efforts are also underway to rejuvenate Medan Pasar and other parts of the historic city centre as Kuala Lumpur seeks to balance development with heritage preservation and the creation of a more liveable urban environment.
